utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. First of all, General Galic, I hope that the reasons for your absence yesterday did not bring any unpleasant surprises, and if there's any reason or if there's any consequence for your ability of being in Court, please inform the Chamber, since I understood that you were away for medical reasons yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I should like to thank you for giving me enough time yesterday to have my medical examination. I don't have any particular news to tell you regarding my health, but I have already informed my counsel, and I am going to inform you about that. I have a problem with wearing a flak jacket. I should like to have your permission to wear a lighter version of the flak jacket, and I think that this would alleviate to a greater extent the problem that I have in my spine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll pay attention to that, Mr. Galic. Please be seated. The second issue I just wanted to touch upon briefly is I did understand that there has been a meeting yesterday between the parties. I hope that there's no news from that, but if this would be otherwise, this would be the moment to inform this Chamber about it. I see nodding twice no news.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, no news is good news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no news is good news. So then I think the Prosecution could call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the next witness for the Prosecution is Baron Aernout van Lynden. He will be taken by Stefan Waespi of the trial team for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Rules require you to make a solemn declaration, of which the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. Would you please make this solemn declaration, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. van Lynden. You will be examined first by Mr. Waespi of the Prosecution team. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My full name is Carel Diederic Aernout Baron van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your place of birth and date?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was born in Kensington, in London, United Kingdom, on the 31st of December, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm a war correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for how many years?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Twenty-two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me briefly take you through your education and professional background experience. You went to school in England and attended military training with the Dutch marines. Did you get any special areas of training?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In university or the marine corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the marine corps.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the marine corps, it was national service for two years, a one-year course as a training to become a second lieutenant, an officer, in the marine corps. And I had training, once I had become an officer, in mortars as a speciality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In 1979 to 1981, you worked for a Dutch newspaper covering the war in Lebanon in the Iraq/Iran invasion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I began journalism in The Hague as you said at the Haagsche Courant on their foreign desk with responsibility for southern Europe and the Middle East. That led to me going to Lebanon where civil war had started in 1975. And in September 1980, I was in Baghdad when Iraq invaded Iran. I then covered that conflict also from the Iranian side. And then in the beginning of 1981, I left the Haagsche Courant and began working as a freelance journalist in the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, as a freelance journalist, you worked from 1982 to 1988, and you've just said in the Middle East. For which media organisations did you work?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I worked for the "Washington Post" newspaper, for BBC Radio, and for the "Observer" newspaper in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then in 1988, you joined Sky News, first as diplomatic and then as a foreign correspondent?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is a 24-hour television news channel based in London. It's -- it goes out via satellite, the Astra satellite and is therefore -- if anyone has a dish, you can watch it throughout Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, you covered for Sky News the revolution in Romania, Lebanon, among many others?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1989, I returned to Lebanon, specifically because of the hostage crisis. In December of 1989, I was in Romania. In 1990 until 1991, I spent seven months in Saudi Arabia covering the crisis and Gulf War. And after that I spent most of my time in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's now go to former Yugoslavia. In 1991, you came for the first time to the Balkans and covered the conflict in Slovenija and Croatia, also Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was sent, just prior to the Slovenian declaration of independence, to Ljubjana and stayed there for several weeks during that initial conflict. When that ended, I returned home first and was then within a matter of days sent to Belgrade, and basically spent most of the rest of that year, with some periods of free time at home, in -- based in Belgrade covering from the Serb side the war that ensued in Croatia. That included many visits to Vukovar. Also included going with the Yugoslav Army to around Dubrovnik and being with militia forces in Banjine and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In this time you just covered, did you have occasion to meet and interview civilians and military leaders?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give a couple of names.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The highest interview I did was with General Karadzic at that time, the commander in chief of the Yugoslav Army. In the field, we met soldiers, militia men, Milan Martic, who was one of the leaders of the Serbs in Croatia; a man who called himself Captain Dragan, a Serb who I think had been born in Australia, although he was never clear to me about that and fought in Banjine and in Krajina; and many soldiers and people of various ranks around Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to talk to Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In July 1991, I was given an interview with Mr. Milosevic, conducted an interview with him. And also spoke to him after the interview when he invited me to join him in a glass of whiskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's now turn to Sarajevo, Mr. Van Lynden. Did you work exclusively for Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did, although that said, Sky News has certain allegiances with other news organisations, specifically the television world in Holland with an organisation called "RTL 4" and the United States with CBS. And therefore, at times these organisations would take my stories or ask me to comment for them. That was not for any extra payment; that was just part of my work as Sky News correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was part of your crew?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The crews, the cameramen, the sound recorders, and the editors, the people who put together the pictures of a story always came from London. So staff members of Sky News, not always exclusively English, Australians, Irish as well. Apart from that, we had producers come from England at certain moments. I was also accompanied also by what we refer to as local producers. These were people of Yugoslav nationality who went with us into the field both to help us, to organise, and of course to help in translation as I don't speak Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo covering the conflict, how often would you make reports? Was it on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was at least once a day. Sometimes depending on the news item, because we are a 24-hour news channel, we have a deadline every hour. And therefore if something happened, we would make more than one report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you may have touched upon that already, but just to make it clear, was Sky News broadcasted in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was visible in the former Yugoslavia, as I've said, if you had a dish. Also in 1991 and I believe into 1992, there was an agreement signed in 1989 between Sky and Yugoslav television whereby the Yugoslav television had the rights to rebroadcast Sky News. And this was certainly done on the third channel in Belgrade throughout 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before we go into details, I would like to know in broad terms the times you were in Sarajevo. Let's start with 1992. First, there was a period between May until August 1992. Where in Sarajevo did you stay?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo in May 1992, I had not been to the city before and initially drove to the presidency. There were no hotels at that stage that were open. And they found a room for me in what had been a government residence for foreign guests, VIPs. It was later turned into the residence of the commander of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. This is a quite low building from which, when there was shelling during the nights, we immediately realised -- my cameraman and myself -- that we couldn't work, we couldn't do the filming. There was also no cellar in which we could hide. And on the second or third day in Sarajevo, we went to what had been the military hospital, which had very badly been shot up at that stage. We met the senior surgeon there, a man called Dr. Abdulah Nakas, and we asked him whether we could stay on the top floor of his hospital which-- where there were no patients. They had been evacuated because it was too dangerous. But where we would in a position to work during the nights to film shelling because right in front of the hospital, you had the Marin Dvor square, the parliament, Grbavica, the Serb-held parts of Sarajevo. To our left, the old part of the city, and to our right the new part of Sarajevo, and it was all very clearly visible. Quite a tall building. And from then on Dr. Nakas agreed that we would be allowed to stay there, and from then on I spent practically every single night when I was in Sarajevo in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you have the editing facilities?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It depended. At various times we had them in different places. Initially the decision had been taken by management in London in May 1992, because practically the entire world press had just fled Sarajevo, that both the editing and our satellite uplink - it's a large dish - to send out the pictures should be -- remain in Pale while we went inside the city. That, however, meant that on a daily basis, my cameraman and I had to cross lines to Ilidza to hand over our tapes and our story, and this was clearly very dangerous. So from -- when we returned later in June to Sarajevo, I had the editing with me. Until early August, we found a base to work from, in the Kosevo Hospital, and after that, when I returned at the end of October 1992, I -- we had a base, a working base within the TV centre at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sarajevo. But as I said, my nights would be spent at what has become known as the State Hospital, the former military hospital of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In September 1992, you were again there for three and a half weeks. Do you know the exact dates?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I don't know the precise dates, no. We -- on that occasion we did not go into Sarajevo, as far as the Bosnian side was concerned. The aim of that mission was to try to cover the war from the Serb side, to also allow the Serbs to speak for themselves as to how they saw the war. I held discussions with Dr. Karadzic in Belgrade prior to going into Bosnia and he agreed that I could come to Pale. He also agreed that we -- that his authorities, his people, would see to it that we would be able to work. We had tried to work previously to that for a few days in -- from Pale, but on each occasion that we sort of stepped in the car, we were immediately arrested and it was impossible to do any work. And then we spent three and a half weeks based in the -- in Pale, in the Pensione Olympic, covering various aspects from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the third period you were in Sarajevo, or covering the conflict in Sarajevo in 1992, was when you returned at the end of October 1992 to Sarajevo. How long did you stay in Sarajevo in that period?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We stayed until, as I remember, the 19th or 20th of December, so just before Christmas, when we left, went to Belgrade, where there were elections, and then went home, had a winter break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in 1993, how long were you covering Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: 1993 I was initially sent into Central Bosnia. I did make some trips into Sarajevo, but always of a rather short nature, so a couple of days, two, three days, and I didn't do the extensive coverage of Sarajevo that I had done in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And very briefly: 1994, what was your presence in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, it was sporadic and usually of a relatively short nature, although I did spend a couple of weeks there following -- in March 1994, following the first market massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's talk in detail about the period September until December 1992. In September 1992, did you interview General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's the position in September? Was it early, was it mid-September?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly the first half of September. When we arrived in Pale, we -- I met Dr. Karadzic again. And as we wanted to have access to the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, it made sense for us to ask for an interview with General Mladic, the commanding officer, because that would give me a chance also to ask General Mladic to give me permission to meet with some of his forces, and that interview was granted; not immediately, but it was granted, and therefore it must have been in the early part, because after that -- it was only after that that we were allowed some access to the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you describe to us the circumstances you met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to come to what was known as the Bosnian Serb Presidency, at that stage a chalet within Pale, which was basically a ski resort. We waited there. As I remember, around the middle of the day, or maybe it may even have been 1.00, General Mladic arrived. He initially, with maps, gave us a rough briefing as to the military situation as he saw it in Bosnia at that time and then suggested that we go elsewhere to conduct the interview proper. Somewhat to our surprise, he then drove to an artillery position of the Bosnian Serbs overlooking Sarajevo, and there the interview was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How far away from Sarajevo is Pale?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that far, but you can't actually -- from Pale, you can't see Sarajevo, but it's - I don't know - a matter of maybe 15 -- directly, 15 kilometres. However, the direct route was closed due to the war, and if you wanted to drive from Pale to Sarajevo, it would take a lot longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court the scenery you saw at the site of the interview?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, the first thing we noticed, really, was that the site was built next to a cemetery, and you walked past that, and then it was an artillery position. He was met by the commander of that position, as I recall, a Potpukovnik , a lieutenant colonel, and there were various pieces of artillery placed not next to each other. They were dug in. It was a prepared position. And they were -- or had been working. There were still bulldozers there preparing further positions at this site. The General didn't mind us filming. We were allowed to film. The only thing that we were requested not to film was the cemetery. So we filmed while he and the lieutenant colonel talked and walked amongst these artillery pieces. There was a wooden table with benches, and that's where we sat down and that's where we conducted the interview, and then below us lay Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many artillery pieces you saw there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't have a precise figure, but it was more than half a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how far away from you were these pieces located?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I mean, we were allowed to walk up to them. That wasn't the point. When we did the interview, they were, I mean, at various distances. They were spread out, as you would expect in an artillery position. Also, because I had actually seen -- when in Sarajevo, I had seen fire coming from this position onto the city, so it was in the line of sight from -- of the Bosnians inside Sarajevo, which made it clear why the Bosnian Serbs had spread out their various pieces, because they could have return fire. So the pieces where we conducted the interview were anywhere between 50 and several hundred metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did the actual interview last?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, more than one tape was used, one tape being 30 minutes, so I would suspect about 40 minutes, something in that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how much, if anything, of this interview was aired?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was certainly aired. Again, as I recall, something like maybe three minutes, which for a news channel, where a bulletin is 30 minutes long, means that one-tenth of the bulletin was given to this story. So it was given quite a lot of prominence, but you don't show it all, because there are other news items in other parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now about the substance of the interview. Do you recall what was said, what he said?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we asked him about the position of what was going on in the war, and he was clearly very confident that he was winning the war and that he felt that the only thing was for them basically to surrender - his opponents I'm referring to - that he had the power to crush them if they did not. When asked what he believed that he was doing, he said, "I'm simply defending my people." His mother still lived in a village in Bosnia. He made that perfectly clear, that he was a Bosnian Serb himself and that he felt that he was defending, as I said, his people. I asked, because it was mooted at the time that a Tribunal of the sort that we find ourselves in today would indeed be opened, whether he was not afraid of being accused of committing war crimes, and he basically laughed it off and said, "Absolutely not." He didn't accept a war crimes Tribunal. He didn't accept that he had committed any kind of war crimes, but that he was, as I said earlier, that he was simply doing his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he say anything about his relation vis-a-vis Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not directly in the interview. When we walked there and we stopped and we looked down, I mean, it was an extraordinary place to be taken, in our opinion. Maybe the Defence attorney could be given some water, Your Honour. There's a lot of coughing going on. I'll continue. When we were walking to the position and we stopped and looked - this is before, prior to the interview - he pointed at the city and then pointed at the palm of his hand and said, "Sarajevo is there." He said, of course, this in Serbo-Croat. As far as I'm aware, General Mladic does not speak any English, and therefore we couldn't communicate directly. But basically he was saying the city was in the palm of his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did you describe General Mladic in your report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My opening sentence was that he was the scourge of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there any reaction at one time from him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was reaction immediately from various people within Pale, some of whom felt that I was blackening their General. But several days after we made the interview, by chance, on the road we ran into -- I mean not literally, but saw the General again, and he was -- seemed to be very happy to see us and laughed about the fact that I had called him the scourge of Sarajevo. He almost felt that it was a title he deserved. I mean, he seemed very happy with the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when was the last time you met General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The last time I met General Mladic was in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was during the crisis, after the first market massacre in Sarajevo, when NATO issued its first ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs. In the end, the crisis was diffused by an agreement that the Bosnian Serbs would withdraw all their heavy artillery and armour from 20 kilometres around Sarajevo, the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. One morning we were - that's to say, my team - was called from the Bosnian Serb Presidency and asked, together with a team from the BBC, to come to the Bosnian Serb Presidency. The other correspondent, the BBC correspondent, John Simpson, and I thought that this was to do a joint interview with Dr. Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb political leader, but in fact it was simply for us to film a meeting of what can be described as the inner or war cabinet of the Bosnian Serbs, and therefore the senior officers of the Bosnian Serb army attended. General Milutinovic, General Gvero, and then General Mladic arrived, and as he arrived, my camera crew and producer were already in the room where the meeting was to take place. John Simpson and I were standing outside, and General Mladic saw me and began, in what was clearly a not very nice manner, to speak to me and then grabbed me in my face, spitting out two words in particular: Zuc and Gorazde. Zuc is a hill north of Sarajevo which, at the end of 1992, was recaptured by the Bosnian forces. I was with those Bosnian forces the day after the capture and did a story on the capture of Zuc, but it is a -- not a huge, but it was a defeat for the Bosnian Serbs, which the Bosnian Serbs never publicly admitted to. And the word "Gorazde" that he uttered referred to the fact that in February 1993 I walked through Serb lines into Gorazde and stayed several weeks there and made a half-hour documentary about this enclave in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you ever met Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, I met him at the London conference that was held; I met him at the beginning of September 1992, prior to my visit that I have been describing to Pale; and I met him several times in Pale in September 1992; and I met him again in February 1994, after the market massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever formally interview him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did, but usually what was the case was Mr. Karadzic, who spoke excellent English, was very willing to speak to my organisation, to Sky News. And therefore what was preferred that he did so directly, either by doing interviews via the telephone with our presenters in London, or live in front of a camera, but being asked the questions from London. The interviews that I did, therefore, in front with the camera were always usually shorter, getting him to answer on one particular point of news or one particular incident. I had long conversations with him, but usually not with a camera. So I never conducted the kind of interview in front of the camera that I had conducted with General Mladic, for instance, or President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why Radovan Karadzic was eager to talk to Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because we could be seen in the region, because he considered us as one of the important international news organisations and seemed to equate us with the position of CNN and of the BBC. And therefore, he felt that it was important to be able to put his point of view on such a channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the course of these discussions you had with him, did Radovan Karadzic ever make a comment about the fate of non-Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He made various comments about Sarajevo, not in the interviews but in general conversations that we had with him, which sometimes lasted for several hours, he made it quite clear that in his opinion Sarajevo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. belonged solely to the Serbs. I remember distinctly him saying that all the ground was actually Serb territory, Serb houses, that it was a Serb city, and it belonged to them and it should belong to them. Then there were moments when he said I am also willing to compromise, and it was his compromise which astounded me at the time, was that a version of the Berlin wall should be built in Sarajevo because he said, of course, we can never live with these people again, and therefore a wall should be built. When I put it to him that this was an outrageous comment given the fact that we were living in what we hoped was a new Europe where the Berlin wall had finally come down, he didn't seem to regard it as outrageous at all. He just kept repeating that he could not ever live with these people. He described -- when I said that they are all the same, the Croats, Serbs, Muslims are all Slav people, he said, and excuse me for swearing, but these are the actual words that I recall, that the Muslims were not Slavs, that they had been "fucked to death by the Turks" and therefore he considered them Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you meet him again in 1994?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Almost immediately on arrival in Pale, I was told to go to the Bosnian Serb Presidency and wait for him there. When he arrived, we waited several hours. His first words were "Oh, no, not Van Lynden", but he then did grant an interview with a camera, but there was no conversation between us prior or after that interview. It was just a question of him sitting in front of the camera answering my questions, and then we were told to leave. I saw him several other instances during that time and during that crisis, but I didn't have any conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did the interview you had with General Mladic have any effect on you being able to visit the troops?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a point away from the camera that we asked General Mladic, we said that we had come there also to put the Serb point of view, I mean, and therefore that it was important to us to be given access to front lines and to Bosnian Serb soldiers. And he agreed. And in the days and weeks following that interview, we did make a number of trips to Bosnian Serb positions, and we were given two military policemen as a -- I mean Bosnian Serb military policemen -- as a permanent escort to see to it that the kind of problems that we had had initially in Pale - at every checkpoint we would always be arrested - that these problems didn't recur.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you filmed military positions, did the officers or other military personnel have any concerns about what you were filming?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It would be extraordinary if they did not. Any officers in any war zone are always concerned with the arrival of television cameras because of a natural fear that we may film certain things that would give away positions to their opponents, specifically, of course, as we came from a television channel and were working for a television channel that could be viewed in the region, anything we filmed. Therefore, my reports could be viewed by all sides. This was always discussed when we went to any kind of position at any time of the war on whichever side we were working on. Generally, we would be taken to company commanders, and a conversation about this would take place. We would make it very clear, usually even we would start the conversation to make it clear to that officer that we were aware of the dangers implicit in giving away any positions, and my cameramen were always also aware of that. So we were very careful in the filming. And I must add that on no occasion have we ever been told by anyone from either the JNA or the Bosnian Serbs that filming that we had done endangered either their men or their positions. The only comment I ever had was from Vukovar that a -- the chief spokesman of the Yugoslav army at that stage was upset that I had shown military debris lying in Sarajevo that had not been cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that's 1991.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you visited these positions in September 1992, in what areas did you go?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We went to various places. In the Serb-held districts within Sarajevo, Grbavica, Hrasno, and the area adjoining what was known as the Jewish cemetery, also on Mount Trebevic where the Serbs had various positions overlooking the city much higher up. I made one, as I recall, two- or three-day journey right the way around the city to Vogosca, to Ilidza, and to Hadzici. So various positions along. At some of these we were told by the military commanders that we went to when we were brought by this escort of two military policemen that they did not want to have us there, and they didn't care what anyone in Pale said about it. In others, we were allowed to work and did, indeed, work and film reports, and everything we filmed was put on air.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps you can start telling us what you saw when you visited the area of Grbavica. Do you recall the date when that trip took place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you say in what part of September that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it was in the middle or later part of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it before or after the interview you conducted with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: After. We didn't get to see any positions before the interview with General Mladic took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you recall how this particular visit was arranged, who accompanied you, who received you at that particular spot?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it was arranged via the Bosnian Serb Presidency in Pale. We had put in these requests, and my producer would go there and talk to them as to what would be possible when. The only escort we had was of these two military policemen and -- who were told where to go and who to see. We began on Mount Trebevic. That was logical. As driving, you would drive over the mountain down towards the Lukavica barracks. And so we stopped on the way, we conducted various interviews with soldiers also higher up on the mountain, saw some of those positions. And then came down into Grbavica. And again, we were taken to a command post usually in a civilian -- formerly civilian building, not into barracks. And there we would meet, as I said, usually a company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How do you know this person was a company commander?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A, they were wearing uniforms; B, they had ranks, either here or sometimes attached. And these were the same ranks that you would see -- that I had seen in the previous year when going to places like Vukovar. These were the old ranks of the Yugoslav National Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for the record indicating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For the record, you just pointed on your right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Both shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on the left shoulder, what was on the left shoulder and what was on the right shoulder?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't precisely recall whether there was a difference. Stars or bars, if they were attached here, indicating that they were lieutenants or captains or majors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did they wear any insignias on their chests?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't always recall them, sorry. There were times when units had other badges on this part of the arm, this part. And they were wearing cap badges. And that had changed because in 1991, this was still the red star. This had now been changed to the white, red, and blue of the Serb, the Serb colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, just for the record again, when the witness said, "There were times when units had other badges on this part of the arm," he showed on to the upper part of the arm just below the shoulder. And in fact, he indicated that this would apply to both arms, left and right.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It could apply only to one, sometimes to both. It differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And also the right chest. Do you recall that -- was anything on the right chest or the left one, or you just cannot tell?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can't recall. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, it's my recollection that when the witness said they had uniforms with ranks either here or sometimes attached, he first pointed at his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And secondly, he pointed at the front of his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: May I just clarify: There are different kinds of uniforms that can be worn. Depends -- the standard JNA uniform would have rank up here on the shoulder. But there were other uniforms -- if there were certain vests, it was a stick-on with velcro of rank. In that case, for instance, a captain would have two bars rather than stars, while he would have had one star here. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you were pointing at your right front chest. Just for the record so that --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't remember whether it was here or here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a matter of the content of your statement. It's just a matter from the transcript, we cannot see where you are pointing at, so that's why we use these words to indicate where you pointed at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the positions you were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As we're discussing the transcript, I thought I heard in one of the languages that the interpreters were asking the speakers to speak a little more slowly and make pauses between question and answer. I think I heard that from the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine since there's no need of English translation that we could not hear that. Mr. Van Lynden, could you please stop, if the words are still moving, wait to answer the question. Otherwise, the translation in the other languages might not be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, can you describe to us, to the Judges, what you saw at this position?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In Grbavica, we were taken into flat buildings to different rooms in these flat buildings at different levels where there were gun placements of various sorts. This includes positions where there were machine-guns, but also other rooms where there were sniper rifles. These were -- I mean, there were sandbags. It was usually dark, and there were only small bits of window left open. These were front-line military positions in an urban war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court one of the sniper rifles? Thank you. Can you please describe to the Court one of these sniper rifles you saw there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they are long-barrelled with wooden stocks. Others that I saw had stocks made of precisely what material I don't -- these are these sort of modern materials. But clearly, long-barreled, not Kalishnikovs, which would be the normal rifle for any soldier to have. And I'm not an expert on sniping, but these -- I had seen sniper rifles in Lebanon and in other parts of the world, and it was clear to me that these were sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there any sights?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were always sights. Any sniper rifle -- sorry, I should have mentioned that. But there were always sights on the top of the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just before you started describing these positions, you said that there were flat buildings. Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, apartment blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Apartment blocks. How many storeys?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Six, seven, up to that. Smaller ones also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And going back now to the equipment you started to talk about, when you mean sights, you mean tel --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Telescopic sights, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any kind of ammunition there in these positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Walking to them, one passed -- although we were not allowed to film this -- mortars with mortar bombs in their cases, in wooden cases standing in courtyards, behind buildings. There was also in this district behind -- as I said, behind buildings away from obviously the direct line Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of fire of their opponents, there was armour of various sorts. Tanks, armoured personnel carriers with machine-guns, and also vehicles with anti-aircraft guns mounted, 30 or 40 millimetre anti-aircraft guns. Inside the buildings, the weaponry was not of such heavy type, nor was the ammunition. The ammunition that we saw was generally of what would be the bullets for a Kalishnikov, but obviously sniper rifles carried a different kind of bullet as far as I'm aware. But we didn't study the ammunition, nor were we allowed to do so. We were allowed -- on one occasion, my cameraman was allowed to try and take a shot through the telescopic sight of one of these rifles, which is -- it's quite a difficult thing to do. But to make it clear that these were front-line positions with sniper rifles. So they did allow us to film that. And on the floor, there were the empty cartridge cases to show that shooting had taken place from these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these positions, did you see just one firing slot or were there several ones?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I saw several in these apartment blocks. We never actually, when we were in these apartment blocks, saw anyone firing, but I heard firing. But we never actually saw anyone firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go to one of these firing slots and look through?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, what one tries to do is to see what the cameraman -- we work in television after all. But yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How far away were the --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were positioned very close to the River Miljacka, which runs right down sort of the middle of Sarajevo. We could see even a bridge crossing the River Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the distance between your position at the time and the Miljacka River?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I can't say precisely, but it wasn't very far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, turning to the soldiers, can you tell us what they were wearing? Perhaps you have somebody particular in your mind and you could describe him to us.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Same kind of uniforms that I had seen the Yugoslav Army wearing around Vukovar. Nearly always, they were wearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make to the form in which the question has been posed because we cannot know whether they were the soldiers of one camp or another camp. So could we be more specific and define what we mean more precisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise, although I did understand that the witness was still telling about what he saw in Grbavica. But if this is -- could you please make that sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we were just talking about these sniper positions, and I would like to ask you to describe one of these sniper ...

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were clearly still in Grbavica. I was describing a soldier of the Bosnian Serb army, and as I was saying, he was wearing precisely the same uniform that the Yugoslav army wore the previous year, and as far as I could see, there was very little difference. Also, as far as the officers were concerned, they were often immaculately turned out. They carried the same bags for maps that I had seen all the officers in the Yugoslav army carry the previous year. As I said, the only difference that I could note at that time was that the Red Star had been taken off and a new badge had been -- with the colours of the flag - white, blue, and red - had been added. Sometimes some of these men were not wearing boots and were wearing sneakers, but we attributed that to the fact that they were not in trenches but were inside buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the observation of the potential target organised, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They -- and again, we're still in Grbavica here. They had walkie-talkies, small radios, and there were clearly other positions higher up or in other buildings, higher up the slope overlooking Sarajevo, who were in contact with these men on the front line positions, spotters, if you like. It was clear that this was co-ordinated. It's not just a man looking through one slit and deciding to do something if he sees something. There were others. It was a co-ordinated effort, as you would expect from a largely -- I mean, at least the officer corps were all professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the communication between the sniper and the spotter would happen how?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Via radio, as I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see ways the snipers protected themselves from Bosnian fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In one apartment building they had put a dummy. Snipers will always try to work from the shadows and never get into the light, and what they had done here was, slightly in the light, build a dummy, in a sort of clownesque type figure, quite large, larger than a man, but with white and red and, as I recall, a sort of plastic black hat, and they joked about this and they were rather proud about this. At another position, not in Grbavica, but a Serb, Bosnian Serb position near the Jewish cemetery, which was -- these were normal civilian houses, or had been prior to the war, where they had used entire tree trunks to protect the building, sometimes on the outside but sometimes also on the inside. What I saw also there, which I had never seen before -- I'd seen various devices used in warfare, but here they had, through a system of using mirrors, it meant that somebody could sit in the corner of the room and, by looking at the mirrors, get a view outside if there was any threat to his position. This was something novel. Again, we were allowed to film that, and I did put that in my report, both the dummy and the use of mirrors. It's quite generally used in any front line position where the opponents are very close, or in an urban war battleground, that people will use some kind of a telescope to keep themselves under cover but while being able to look what is happening in the terrain in front of them, but this use of mirrors was a novel one for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall the date or the time, approximate or accurate, that you saw those mirrors?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I said, these were during the same number -- we went down into the Bosnian Serb side of Sarajevo on several days. It takes time before commanders give you permission to film, and then you have to get to a building and then you have to see what you can film. We didn't, therefore, do it all in one day, so it went over several days of visits to Grbavica, Hrasno, and to the positions by the Jewish cemetery. But this, as I said before, was around the middle, towards the latter half of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, have you attended an incident which involved a machine-gun position?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. When we were taken to Hrasno, we were taken to a position somewhat higher up than the apartment block that I was referring to earlier in Grbavica, and there the gun emplacement was not inside the house but had been dug in the garden outside the house. While my producer and I were still speaking to the officer who had taken us to this position, my cameraman and sound recordist had gone to this gun position with two Bosnian Serb soldiers, or two Serb soldiers. There they had a machine-gun. While one man manned the machine-gun, the other looked down with binoculars. And according to my local producer, one of these men, the man who manned the machine-gun itself, was not actually Bosnian Serb but was recognisable through his accent as coming from southern Serbia, specifically the Nis area. And this man at a certain moment opened fire. As I said, I was not at the position itself. We were about 20 metres away from it, talking to the officer who had brought us there. When we asked what he had shot at, his answer was, "The Mujahedin," by which he meant his opponents, the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see any Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I did make -- well, I did make the point that having been in Afghanistan, I didn't see any Afghans running around, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that the soldier at the machine-gun was from Serbia, the Nis area. Can you describe to the Court the way he looked like, what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was wearing, once again, the same uniform that the Yugoslav National Army wore. As I recall, he had a moustache, and he was certainly not the youngest. I mean, he must have been in his 40s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said earlier that the company commander -- or that the commander showed you around at this point. Perhaps you can clarify that, if I'm right or -- what was his -- do you know where he was from? Was he also from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is at the Hrasno position, and we did see different commanders, depending on which sector one visited, and one was taken by different officers to these various locations. And as I recall, the man manning the machine-gun is the only one that my producer, who, Your Honour, studied linguistics at Belgrade university but was -- partially his mother was from Croatia, his father from Montenegro, and he was actually born in Bosnia. This man was very much aware of the different accents within the former Yugoslavia. As I recall, the only time he made mention of someone not coming from Bosnia was with this one machine-gun. All the others were, as I recall, Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, you may not be precise enough. Can you tell us the date this incident happened in Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I can't. It's -- as I said earlier already, it's in this general period, in the middle of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident on Miljacka River which involved an old lady?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This was when we were within these flat buildings in Grbavica, where at one of these positions my cameraman, while filming, suddenly saw an old lady appear and cross one of the bridges - a footbridge; not a major bridge, but a footbridge - across the river Miljacka to -- from the Bosnian Serb side to the Bosnian side. We, of course, asked about this. There was no fire. And the soldiers had clearly been informed that this was going to take place. We had not been informed beforehand. We were surprised about this, but they said that this had been worked out with the other side, that this elderly lady, certainly over 60 years old, they said she was a Muslim and that she should be allowed, after a deal, to cross from their side. One of the soldiers then made the remark, "We don't want any of them with us. They all have to leave."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We talked about sniper positions. Can we look at the other side? Can you tell us about hot spots, I mean areas which were particularly dangerous for the population?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Now, to make it -- if I may just make it clear, also to the Defence attorney. There were positions held on the Bosnian Serb side, specifically within Grbavica, which were dangerous there, where people living there still could come under sniper fire, but much more so on the other side in Sarajevo, where, because of the terrain, because Sarajevo is an elongated city lying in a valley along the river Miljacka, and because the Bosnian Serbs held the high ground, they were in positions to literally shoot down streets within the new part of Sarajevo and within the central part of Sarajevo. And places like Marin Dvor square, much of the length of the Marsal Tito Bulevar, the main road in Sarajevo, were open to sniper fire. And also there was one specific turning -- when one -- quite close to the Bosnian Presidency, where there was often sniper fire and where, in the end, the Bosnian government erected a sort of wall with -- using containers, so that people could walk behind these and not be a potential target. There were areas in the region known as Skenderija - this is Bosnian-held territory, but on the other side of the river Miljacka - which could also come under fire, and a number of the bridges in the Skenderija area and further, also a bridge made famous in June 1914 with the assassination of the Austrian Crown Prince, Franz Ferdinand. This bridge also could come under Bosnian Serb fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware of any warning signs in these notorious areas you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not initially. When I initially went into Sarajevo in May 1992, there were not warnings, but later on there were. And as I said, later on, also the Bosnian authorities tried to take some measures to protect civilians, specifically those on foot, from going through these areas. What was also done was in many of the smaller streets, that they would try to find carpets or something to hang in the street, so therefore to prevent direct sight from the higher positions, from the Bosnian Serb positions, from fire in these streets, but that could, of course, only be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. done in relatively narrow streets. Marin Dvor square was always an impossibility. But at these points you would then see a warning that there could be a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what it exactly said?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid -- as I said, I'm afraid I'm not a linguist. I didn't learn Serbo-Croat, apart from a few words. There was "sniper," and as I recall, it was spelled in a different manner. We would in English spell it s-n-i-p-e-r, and I think -- there was an "a" in it, and maybe an "a" and a "j." But it was written in the Roman rather than in Cyrillic writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were they written on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, usually on cardboard or pieces of wood about that size, 50 centimetres by 50 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described the tour you made visiting positions of the Bosnian Serb army. How many of these tours did you make?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Inside -- in September 1992, inside the Bosnian Serb-held areas of Sarajevo, as I recall, we were there for maybe three days. We made a number of other tours, as I mentioned earlier, also around Sarajevo, to various other points, but this is further away from the city, to the north of the city and to Ilidza. So there were a number of tours. In total, visiting with the Bosnian Serbs army, maybe we spent something like ten days in all, but there were other stories to be done as well, of a civilian nature, as far as medical care was concerned, stories of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just said you have toured around all these positions, you have talked to soldiers and commanders. Of all the snipers you have seen, were they under the command and control of the Bosnian Serb army or not, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have absolutely no doubt that all the soldiers that we saw were working within a fairly strictly controlled hierarchical army. As I said, we would always go to a command post first. The commanders that we met were always well attired, professional officers of the Yugoslav army, as far as I could see. There was no difference between the officers I met in 1991 and the officers that I met in places like Grbavica in 1992. And the men formed part of an organised army and were under clear military orders. Not all the soldiers that we met were professionals. I mean, many of these were conscripts, and the Yugoslav National Army, of course, had been a conscript army. But there is no doubt to my mind that they were part of, as I said, a controlled military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to another subject. Was there an incident you witnessed when an apartment block was on fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You're referring to an incident in Sarajevo, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That incident was when I returned to Sarajevo - this time not on the Bosnian Serb side but on the Bosnian side - at the end of October, 1992, the incident took place on the 5th of December, 1992, as I now recall. But which in my initial statement I had said had taken place in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why do you recall it was the 5th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because I am a dutchman, and in Holland, we have something called Saint Nikolas on the 5th of December, and it was only later that I remembered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the exact location that incident took place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The exact location possibly not, but it was an apartment block along the Marsal Tito Bulevar, and it's -- how should I describe? I don't have a map here. If you have a map, then I can maybe try to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think that can certainly be arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that we are using the original, unmarked black and white map? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honours. I think the map with the Exhibit Number P3648 could be suitable to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we first have to sort out some technical difficulties with the screen, but it has been solved by now. Madam Registrar, the number just mentioned, is that the unmarked original map since if we do need any additional markings, we should have a new exhibit number for it, although we start, then, with the same unmarked black and white map.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you please express yourself in English. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As soon as you have found the appropriate spot, if you could mark it with a blue pen with a cross.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: If I can first do this, Your Honour, and just explain as I see it the various places that I'm referring to. What I'm pointing to now, this was the former Marsal Tito barracks, evacuated by the Serb army -- at the beginning of June 1992. Next to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, whenever the witness points at a certain spot indicating what this spot is, would you please invite him to mark it because otherwise -- and do we have a blue marker? Not the black one. Yes, that's important because the black marker is for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Van Lynden, if you could mark in the middle of what you just pointed out with maybe a "T" indicating that you said it was the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps you can outline the building with a big circle around.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Alongside it, as I said, runs what was known as the Marsal Tito Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps you can also mark it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps you can indicate in the middle of it a "B" indicating that that is the Marsal Tito Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: And as I recall, the building that came under fire was roughly in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you just make a circle.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And indicate maybe the letter Y.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, perhaps later we can return to the map. Mr. Van Lynden, how come you were at that location?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had spent the previous night with the chief of the Sarajevo Fire Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall his name, by the way?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid I don't. I'm not very good at recalling names. And we -- because we had been planning to do a story on the fire brigade and the problems that they encountered in their work, as it happened that night, there were no fires. And the fire brigade did not have to leave their headquarters. And in the morning, we then returned to our working base, which at that time was in the TV centre, which entailed us to drive down the Marsal Tito barracks in the direction of the airport through Marin Dvor Square, past the Marsal Tito barracks. And it was after that we saw, as we were driving, that there was a fire in this apartment block. In front of the apartment block, actually on the street side, was a lower building where shops had been located prior to the war, and we were able to park our car behind those buildings because we saw as we arrived that incendiary bullet rounds were still continuing to be fired at this building, and it was these incendiary bullet rounds that had caused these fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can briefly return to the map, can you indicate on the map with an arrow which directions these incendiary rounds as you call them were fired from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, you can indicate again with the blue pen, just making an arrow from the areas you thought the fire originated into the area you described as a Y.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: May I just make the point to the Court that this is very rough because when a position that you're at is being actually shot at, there is no reason for a journalist to stick his head up to try and find out precisely where the gun is. You just don't do that. So I don't have a precise position, but it was coming from that side, coming over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, how far away from the confrontation lines south was the building located?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Maybe a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall from --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Maybe a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall from which side of the confrontation lines the fire originated?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From the Bosnian Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your opinion, was this apartment block you just described a military or civilian target?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A civilian target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I come to that conclusion because we saw a lot of civilians there. We spoke to them, and these people lived in this apartment block. They had had their homes there. We filmed one man who was distraught because all his possessions were lost in one of the fires, and there were several different fires in this apartment block had been lost. We talked to people also to check whether any outgoing fire had gone from this apartment block. Civilians in any war zone are always very wary of their property being used by the military in any way whatsoever because they are afraid that their opponents will then fire on that property. And the civilian population in Sarajevo was no different to anywhere else. And it would have been made -- we would have found out if that building was being used by units of the Bosnian Army to fire on the other side. Everybody said that there had been no fire, that they had been in the apartment block. And the first thing that they knew anything was happening was when the first incendiary rounds, and they were from the beginning incendiary rounds, were fired at this apartment block.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just said a sentence ago there had been no fire, by that you meant no outgoing fire. Now, do you know how many civilians lived in that apartment block?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, and I don't have a precise title -- a precise figure. But, I mean, it was quite a big building. And I imagined that several hundred people will have lived in that apartment block.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians getting out of the apartment block while the fire was on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe a little bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I saw -- sorry. I saw men, women, and children leaving the apartment block. But using not the entrance towards the Marsal Tito Bulevar, but on the other side of the building where they were not under direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you film the incident?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a time that the fire brigade came?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they came after we had arrived there. But yes, they did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was the building still fired at while the fire brigade attended the fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was again fired at, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we are at 10.30 now, and I would like to have our first break. Would you please find a suitable moment for this break. And apart from that, may I remind you, as you might know, this Chamber assists the parties in keeping a close eye on the clock, that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. used considerably more than 50 percent of your time estimate for this witness. So if you would please find a suitable moment, or when this is a suitable moment, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Yes, I have also passed more than half of my examination-in-chief. And we will play the video of this incident I think right after the break. So I think it will be a convenient time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be then a suitable moment. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I see that your colleague, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is not there. Is there any reason why we should not proceed, or do you expect him to come soon?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect my colleague any minute. He's still in the Defence room. It's possible that he has problems getting out. The doors were locked a moment ago when I was there. But that should not be a problem. I think we can start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed, unless there's any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, just one or perhaps two questions before we see the video. Was there further firing into the building after the firemen had successfully extinguished the fire or part of the fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They hadn't yet extinguished all the fires, but there was more incendiary rounds fired into the building, yes. Firing continued while the firemen were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And compared to the location of the firemen, where did the additional incendiary rounds go to? Below or above or beside?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Below, as far as we could witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the video could now be played. It's about, I think, a minute clip, and there is a transcript which has been served to the Defence, I think also to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not remember that we received a transcript of the video. Oh, the registrar says we have, so this is -- oh, it has -- it's available to us now. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just for your information, we only show the part where the building is seen on fire, and that begins with -- after the Egyptian colonel. We won't show that. Just it starts with van Lynden, and then the second paragraph, van Lynden. So it's not the whole transcript but only the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at 5:56, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the video could be shown now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: VAN LYNDEN: ... mirrored by the reality in the city. Serb incendiary rounds, setting a string of flats ablaze in one apartment block. A resident watches, distraught, his home and belongings gone. Seconds later, further bursts of incendiary rounds crash into the building or bounce off the wall into the street below. Wanton arson on a purely civilian target. As ever, Sarajevo's remarkable firemen fight back, getting their hoses to the flames for once unhampered by a cut in the water supply. But for the fire chief, water is not the main concern. His engines are running out of fuel and he tells us that he won't be able to cope with another fire this day. The fall of Otes and escalation of shelling here in the centre of Sarajevo again underline the impotence of international efforts in Bosnia. Ceasefires and political talks have led nowhere and won't until the western world proves it has a true commitment in ending this war. Aernout van Lynden, SkyNews, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, do you recognise this clip?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that the footage which you had prepared for Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The footage, all that, the shots of the firemen, the shots of the building from the ground were taken by George Davis, a Sky News cameraman. The shots from further away when you see the building sideways were taken from a cameraman of CNN from the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was the elderly man on the clip?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was a resident of this apartment block.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's to say my producer talked to him. It was not a man who spoke English or German or French or any other language that I'm capable of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you talked to him and the other civilians at that scene. Did they tell you what their feelings were?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, obviously they were distraught. They were also fearful. I mean, those who were in the apartment block when the shooting began and came out, then you are afraid, of course. Also, there was a clear sense of -- I would call it impotence on their part. They feel that they cannot do anything. They are no longer in control of their own lives, and things are happening to them outside control. Most of us in our daily lives try in one manner or another to have some control over the lives we lead. These people in this situation no longer had that control, and that could lead to a real feeling of despair. Of course, they also suffered in other ways. They couldn't get the food, the water, nor the heat. And this was already -- Sarajevo was turning cold. So there were further reasons for their despair. But certainly when a building that you've lived in and where you've built up a home is then targeted in this manner, then obviously there is a great feeling of anger. But above all, of despair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us how large these incendiary rounds were? Were they small ones or were they larger ones? Do you have an opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as -- I mean, it's -- obviously, you don't pick one of them up. But as you saw in the footage, one of them hit the building and then bounced back directly over the heads of my cameraman and myself. I was standing next to my cameraman when that happened. It's difficult to say precisely, but these were roughly 15 centimetres, I would say. 10 to 15 centimetres.
