utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And given your military background, can you indicate to us what sort of weaponry would have fired an incendiary round you've just described of that size?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I should point out that in the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps, we do not have incendiary rounds. I was aware that the Yugoslav Army did and had seen them use these. You are talking from heavy machine-guns or anti-aircraft guns. I mean this is quite large millimetres. This is not from a standard Kalishnikov rifle, as far as I'm aware. I'm not an expert on incendiary rounds because as I said, during my military time we in the Netherlands do not have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's talk now about a different subject. You had described already artillery pieces you had seen when you interviewed General Mladic. Just very briefly, have you seen other weaponry capable of shelling?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. As I think I have already described, on the road that you take from Pale to get to Grbavica or Hrasno, you go over Mount Trebevic and there were Serb positions there on which we did see heavier weaponry, above all, mortars. And also inside the city, we saw mortars of various calibre’s up to 120 millimetre. And I think I have already described that I saw tanks that were stationed behind buildings in the Bosnian Serb-held areas and which were occasionally used. I should add that I never saw with my own eyes them being used. The only heavy vehicle that I actually saw and that we filmed being used was an armoured personnel carrier with a heavy machine-gun mounted on top of it, and that heavy machine-gun fired towards the other side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Truck-mounted, usually two-barreled guns, again, used in a similar fashion to the armour in that they would be hidden behind buildings and then brought out for use. But I never saw one actually firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you have seen the topography of Sarajevo. You were standing there with General Mladic. You have also been inside the city. Again, from your experience there in Sarajevo, from your training, what's the effect of topography on the use of auto weaponry use, in particular shelling?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Obviously, for anyone bringing down heavier fire, either with mortars or with artillery, the fact that you have direct sight, that you have direct observation, makes it much more easy to have this fire accurate. Anyone who is using artillery or mortars will tell you that it will take at least three shells, unless you are very, very lucky, to hit the target. Usually one shell will land too far or too short from its target. The next one will overshoot in the opposite direction, and therefore it's only the third that is likely to hit its target. It may take more. But if you cannot actually see the target, and which, of course, is possible with artillery that you are firing over a hill, it's more difficult to observe. And the observers would have to be in a different position. Often, with the topography of Sarajevo, the Serb gunners could directly see themselves what they were firing at. And therefore, it made the situation quite different to those that I experienced in Beirut at the various fronts during the Iran/Iraq war, or in other places in Bosnia. Sarajevo was extraordinary as far as that's concerned because of the Serb control of the high ground all the way around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever see mortar being used against a moving target?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we believe we did in the sense that we were the target. Driving several times along the Marshal Tito Bulevar, we noticed mortar bombs impact in front of or behind our vehicle. And it was my opinion that what was happening was that the people in the hills above could clearly see us moving and could work out how long it would take us from getting from Point A to Point B. And would then put a mortar bomb in, i.e., in a sense sniping with mortars. That's what I personally believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described earlier just a few minutes ago the way artillery is supposedly to be used, different steps, different shells, and moving back and forwards. Have you seen the Bosnian Serb army using this tactic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's not a tactic; it's the way you use artillery to hit the target that you're aiming for. So you need observers. And it is unlikely, unless you are very lucky, as I said before, that you hit your target immediately. Specifically, in June 1992, from the vantage point that we had in the building as we've described before, the former military hospital now known as the State Hospital, I was able to see concentrated Serb artillery fire on the Marshal Tito barracks that had been evacuated by the Serb forces. And there what we saw was that the initial shells landed long on the railways behind the barracks, and then were brought on to the barracks, and then they found their target, and then there was concentrated fire on that target. It was our opinion that in their evacuation of the Marshal Tito barracks, they had not been able to withdraw all their equipment. They wanted to clearly destroy the equipment they had left behind and destroy the base. It was extremely sustained fire which often went on all night. It continued for several days. And it was, on the whole, extremely accurate once the gunners had found their range, i.e., once after the initial shells had landed long, they had brought the shells on to the target. But simultaneously, absolutely simultaneously, I have seen fire raining down all over Sarajevo, not in this same concentrated manner, which was clearly just shell fire directed at the city with no military purpose, because if it had had a military purpose, it would have been sustained fire at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were talking about the period of June, I assume, 1992. Have you seen similar fire you just described later, when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At any period that we were in Sarajevo, apart from when I was there in March 1994, there was always shell fire, but I have never witnessed the kind of intense bombardment as -- and concentrated bombardment as of the Marsal Tito barracks, apart from in June 1992. It was sporadic, it was a few shells here and there, but it was never the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. kind of sustained fire that we saw then, and therefore it was our opinion that this was fire not directed at a military goal but simply at the city and the people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the effect of this system of firing you've just described on the population, civilian population in the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The effect was to cause fear with anyone, because people feared that whenever you went outside your house, you could -- you were in danger; you were never safe. Even if there was a building between you and the Serb forces, it meant that, with artillery or with mortars, you could always be hit, because there was fire everywhere, and therefore people were always afraid when they were outside. To a certain degree, humans are adaptable and they get used to this. People learn to live with it. But there was always fear whenever you went outside, and that was the case for us as well. I mean, we had initially normal Volkswagen Golfs. Later on we had armoured Land Rovers. But we always realised that any trip, you were always taking a risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different, although related, subject, the utilities. Who had, in your opinion, control over the utilities from mid-September 1992 on? Perhaps even earlier, but I'm asking you specifically about that period.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As the city was besieged, I believe that the control was in the hands of those doing the besieging, that is, therefore, the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how about access to food and other basic utilities of daily life for the civilian population? Did you ever make a report about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, on various occasions. A city, of course, doesn't grow its own food. It has to be brought in from outside. And therefore, once a city is under siege, food becomes a scarce commodity, and you could see that if you went to the markets. There were no shops left by the time I arrived in Sarajevo in May 1992, or in the sense that they were closed because they were empty, and the food that was available had to be brought, in general, from outside. Of course, people, as the war progressed and as the siege continued over three and a half years, those lucky enough to have a spot of garden tried to grow some vegetables for themselves, but many of the people of Sarajevo lived in apartment blocks and therefore were not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there running water for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. In that sense, that sometimes there was, but for long periods there was not, and therefore that meant that people had to leave their houses or apartments to fetch water at other points. But within the homes there was often not running water. Even in the hospital it was often a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What about in Pale?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In Pale, there were at times electricity cuts, but there was always running water during those periods that I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever make a report about the malnutrition of children?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not only of children. What we looked at was how did the effect of siege and the kind of diet -- I mean, a war diet affect the civilian population. That meant that we interviewed the UNHCR that was bringing in food, who immediately admitted that on no single day had they been able to bring in enough food to feed the civilian population. And we talked to professors, nutrition experts, people who dealt with the immunity system and how the immunity system and people's -- the strength of people's immunity system had been affected by not eating enough. And also it included a visit to the chief of the maternity part of the Kosevo, the academic hospital of Sarajevo, who showed us figures that, in his opinion, because the mothers were undernourished, there were more stillborn babies, that this had more than doubled since the siege began - and this report was done towards the end of 1992 - and that more children were born who were underweight, let us say. And again, he also reiterated the fact that the immune system had been -- the strength of the immune system had decreased because people were not getting enough food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. You said that you stayed a considerable amount of your time in the State Hospital in terms of accommodation. Was it shelled? And in particular, I'm interested in: Was it ever shelled by multi-rocket launchers, or targeted?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The former military hospital is in the direct sight and line of fire of - or was - of the Bosnian Serb forces, and at the beginning of the war, even before I arrived in Sarajevo, it was repeatedly targeted. It was also targeted with heavy weaponry. I can't say which -- when I saw rooms that had been hit by heavy weaponry, whether this was an artillery shell or what you call a multiple rocket launcher. While staying there, I did see multiple-rocket-launcher fire coming from the top of the mountains around Sarajevo and falling very close to the hospital. This is the period that I have already described after the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks. And there were certain moments that when we were filming this at night, we feared that the hospital was going to get hit. As far as I'm aware, it was not hit at that stage. The only larger projectile, apart from gunfire, that hit the hospital while I was actually in it occurred at the end of -- towards the end of 1992, when the hospital, which had a generator and therefore functioning electricity and lifts, and I was about to take the lift to the top floor when there was an extremely large explosion and one of the lift shafts was hit, and we believe that that was from tank fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned the multi-rocket launchers that were firing. Do you recall when that was, when you observed that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: June 1992. It was -- they were clearly visible then, and we filmed them both in day and during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you seen them later as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The multiple rocket launchers, no, not that I can recall now. There was artillery fire certainly. But I should maybe explain to the Court that to most people it would seem a simple thing for a journalist, for a television camera to film. But artillery fire, unless it is sustained in one place, is extremely difficult to film. One shell landing here and another shell landing 500 metres away makes it very difficult work for the cameraman. We saw periods of extremely intense fire in which the whole of Sarajevo, it seemed to us, came under fire, specifically in the early days of June 1992. At other periods we did witness and see fire on several districts, but it was never as intense, nor was it concentrated fire. It was one or two, possibly rockets, more likely artillery shells, that landed in one district. This was practically impossible for us to film, and therefore we do not have the video evidence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While you were at the hospital, State Hospital, did you ever see a sniper operating therefrom, or any other indications, like spent cartridges, ammunition, that snipers were operating at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I'm also -- when we first visited the hospital, and my cameraman and I decided that this would be a good base, we were very careful in checking whether this was in any way being used by the military, because if we were going to set up a base on the top floor, we didn't want to be on the top floor of a military establishment. And we looked around. I even went up on the roof itself, which was quite hazardous, because then you are in the line of fire. I could be observed up there. I found no spent cartridges at any time, nor any military personnel inside the hospital, apart from those brought in as casualties of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you been at in the Jewish cemetery in the first part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I mean not actually in the cemetery because the cemetery was a "no man's land" in a no-go area. But from both sides, from within the city, from the Bosnian side therefore, we shall able to get to positions to film it. And later on, as I described, in September 1992, and again in February 1994, we were taken to the area on the Bosnian Serb side, and I was able to see it then. I mean, the graves were clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the Jewish cemetery or the surroundings in -- the first time, did somebody accompany you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When I went the first time was when I was inside the city. This was in May 1992. And yes, we were accompanied by, as I recall, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you ever meet Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of a man calling himself such. He also called himself Vojvoda we were told. But the meeting was very short because on seeing me, he pulled out his gun and told that if we didn't leave, he would shoot me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was Aleksic? You said he was a warlord. Why did it come about that you wanted to meet him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't think I called him a warlord.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He called himself or his people called him a Vojvoda. What had occurred was that we were in Pale. I was based in Pale. NATO had issued its first ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs in conjunction to the situation in Sarajevo which followed after the market massacre. We heard that one of the troops of Mr. Aleksic had been killed, and that there would be a funeral. With what is known as a minder, a member of the Bosnian Serb so-called Ministry of Information, and with my crew, at that time a wholly Serb crew, a cameraman from Belgrade and a producer from Belgrade, we went down to Grbavica and then drove along towards the Jewish cemetery to what our minder said was the headquarters of Mr. Aleksic. And there, we found that he was not there, but men that he commanded and who said that they were commanded by him said that we should wait. This included a number of Russians who said that they had volunteered for the war, and even one Japanese gentleman who described himself as a Japanese Chetnik, referring to the name of Serb nationalists who had fought in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion as to which command --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion under which command and control Aleksic and his soldiers were from what you saw at that time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Unlike the other soldiers that I have described previously, these people were not wearing JNA uniforms. They were dressed in various ways. Some of the weaponry I saw was not Kalishnikovs but other types of weaponry, G3s, rifles produced in the west rather than in the former Yugoslavia, which had a large arms industry. But I have no doubt at all, and this was also confirmed to us by the minder from Pale, that these men were under the control of the Bosnian Serb army, and that they were not a freelance unit doing whatever they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I said, this was a Bosnian Serb talking to me who had been in the Bosnian Serb armed forces, which he admitted to us. Apart from that, at this time, firing had ceased. There were negotiations going on. And it could be that a unit that was not under military control would break these rules. As far as I'm aware, also from what we heard afterwards, at no time at that time was the cease-fire broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What did the minder from Pale actually say? Do you recall his words?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When I asked who does this man fall -- I mean under whose command, he said, "Under the commanders of the army in this district".

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The market massacre you referred to a couple of minutes ago, do you mean by that the Markale shelling incident of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'm about to conclude in a few minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In that time, did you ever cross Marin Dvor Square? And I can maybe make it more precise in terms of dating. After February 1994, the peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a peace agreement, but an accord was reached whereby Russian forces of UNPROFOR went into the Serb-held districts of Sarajevo whereby the Bosnian Serb forces agreed to withdraw their heavy armour and artillery in the so-called 20-kilometre exclusion zone, or to leave their armour at collection points manned by UNPROFOR. And all shooting in Sarajevo stopped. I had been initially in Pale. After this agreement was reached, I went into Sarajevo. And in March did, indeed, for the first time during the war walk across Marin Dvor Square, which would have been a ridiculous thing to do at any other time. But we were not fired at and we were not in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the position -- or what would have been the danger of crossing Marin Dvor? To what positions was it exposed to, in your opinion or experience? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Marin Dvor Square was always one of the most dangerous places to be in Sarajevo. We always drove very quickly, indeed. For those staying at the Holiday Inn, which I never did, it was always a dangerous place to get into. There was an underground parking, but practically always there was fire every single day on Marin Dvor Square from the Bosnian Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you specify from which part of the Bosnian Serb positions would Marin Dvor be observed or fired at?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now just one or two more questions, Your Honour, to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one deals with your colleagues. How many journalists worked in Sarajevo, and where were they from, in the times you have been there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When I initially went into Sarajevo, as I think I previously said, there were very few journalists left. Most of them had fled from the city. There were a few photographers left from England, America, and New Zealand, as I recall at the time. Other periods, there were hundreds of journalists in Sarajevo. And I imagine that if you take the war as a whole and the three and a half years of siege as a whole, then probably thousands of journalists passed through Sarajevo from all over the world, specifically from Europe, but from every single continent. There were Japanese journalists, Americans, South Americans, but those permanently there were usually from Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question would be, after all you have said, and based also on the visits you made to the troops, discussions with the soldiers and officers, did you come to a conclusion about the discipline of the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I made some conclusions, yes. That the officers were professional officers of the JNA, that they try to keep their men under control. One problem that they did have was the fact that there was somewhat, to my amazement, always alcohol at most of these positions. And this, of course, is not a good thing as far as discipline is concerned if someone has drunk a lot of Slivovitz or rakija, you are less likely to be so disciplined. This was a problem also we had noticed at other times in other places, both during 1991 and in other parts of Bosnia. Also, many, of course, of the normal soldiers were, as I said before, they were conscripts; they were not professionals. Not all of them were particularly happy about being there. But the officer corps was professional, knew what it was doing, and most of the time the soldiers themselves did come under that discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps to conclude, if the witness could be shown the map again. And I also have a correction to make about the map. I'm told by my case manager that the number -- but we could perhaps at the same time bring the map -- the map is there already. The correct number would be P3644.VL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the original number given and added the name of the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, if you could indicate the Marin Dvor Square and the Jewish cemetery. And again, if you could mark them in blue, perhaps with an "M" where Marin Dvor Square is, and a "J" where the Jewish cemetery is located.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, this has to be on this side of the Miljacka River. It is on the southern side of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For the record, the witness just made a "J" with a quite harsh little corner as opposed to a smooth "J", and he makes an arrow to the southeastern direction indicating that it should be moved into a southern direction. And please, could you draw a circle around that Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he just indicated now a circle around this arrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the examination-in-chief. We will, I understand, tender the exhibits after cross-examination or any eventual re-examination, unless you direct otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The admission into evidence of the map shown until now will finally be decided upon after cross-examination and, if necessary, re-examination of the witness. Ms. Pilipovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. With your authorisation actually, I would like to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's up to the Defence team who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, Ms. Pilipovic will possibly have a few additional questions. However, the problem we have is a technical problem, Mr. President, and I would like to tell you about it. The witness has indicated certain things which meant that I went to the Defence Chamber in order to get the material which I had in my laptop. However, the -- there has been a problem with the printer, so now things that I had to print I was not able to do since these pieces of evidence [as interpreted]. And thanks to the Prosecution, would it be possible -- since I had technical problems with printing, would it be possible to have another piece of evidence? And I have a reference number naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I changed from language, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so I'll just try to read. I lost a few lines. Yes. Could the Prosecution assist? I mean, I do understand that it's a matter of just printing or having printed some documents. Would it be possible for you to proceed, or just write on a piece of paper numbers of pages that you would like to have printed? And perhaps the Prosecution team could assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could describe what kind of exhibit you would like us to print and also give exact details, date or any number the Prosecution has attached to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It's just one page, and the number is ERN R004-46717. It is a letter signed by General Morillon. The letter is addressed to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. And this is for technical reasons that I have to require, if you would be so kind to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Prosecution will assist you. So the number is clear to you? The number is not clear? I would invite you just to write it down on a piece of paper and give it to the Prosecution so that there will be no misunderstanding. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, hello. Thank you for coming here as a witness. You gave us a statement. The first statement that I'm going to refer to, is this a statement that was taken on the 8th and 10th of May, 2001, and on the 28th and 29th of September, 2001?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware of this statement that you're referring to. Can we get my screen away from the map and back to the -- thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is this -- was this a draft or was this your definitive statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was a partial statement written up by an investigator of this Tribunal. It's not a statement written by me, no. I haven't written my book yet about the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So just to make things clear: As we read this statement, this written statement, terms like, and I'm quoting, "war of terror," and these are terms used by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. Those were also words used by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I heard in your answer "equally." Can you confirm -- "also words used by myself." Could you answer by yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explain what he said, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You can't force him to say yes or no. Some things are a bit more complicated than just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What I was trying to say was that the investigator wrote down words I had used. A phrase like "war of terror" was a phrase used by me. But the statement is not, I mean, my full memoirs of what I witnessed during either 1991 or thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You stated a moment ago -- and I am referring here to page 28, line 16. I believe that was 10 hours, 3 minutes, 57 seconds. In answering to a question, you said that the snipers were firing on Mujahedins. Is this the way you recall it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We asked -- this is the man with the machine-gun in Hrasno that had opened fire. We asked him what he had been shooting at, and his answer was he had been shooting at the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, is it true to say that in your written statement that we just referred to, you said, and I'm quoting, "shooting at Mujahedin snipers"? And I'm insisting on the word "snipers." I can let you see your own statement if you like.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't have the statement in front of me, but if that's -- if you say that that's what I've written, then that's -- and that -- I had obviously signed this statement, then that must be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that you quote literally this part so that the Prosecution can check on the part of the statement you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you like, I can let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... read it out. If you just indicate the page and then the Prosecution can verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting, in page 12. This is from a statement which we have referred to, and I'm now quoting: [In English] "What they were shooting at was ..." Sorry. "It." "I was given the stock phrase that they were merely shooting at Mujahedin snipers." [Interpretation] I am repeating: [In English] "Shooting at Mujahedin snipers." [Interpretation] At the end of page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is the following: The answer that you were given, that they were, therefore, shooting at snipers from the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one point. Perhaps my friend could quote the whole sentence and starting with "When asked what ..." So the witness sees it in context or -- and not just one or two words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible for you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to quote a bit more of the context? But of course, we can't just read the whole page. Is there any relevance in the -- if you've got the context in front of you, could you please indicate what exactly you would like to -- where to start and where to stop and how many lines these will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole sentence. Okay. Please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please quote in the context as asked by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I just did, but I can do it again. And if you like, I can read the previous sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask the Prosecution to tell you exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So this is the last paragraph on page 12 of your statement, which says the following: [In English] "They had been given orders that allowed them to engage targets of their choice. When asked what they were shooting it" - I read it as it is - "it --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "At."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "At." I read as it is. "... at, I was given the stock phrase that they were merely shooting at Mujahedin snipers." Of course, it's "at" instead of "it," but that's something ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put your question to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I read "it" because that's what it says, but the question is the following: So it is true to say that in the answer to the question that you asked, you were told that these soldiers were firing at snipers, not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just at Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. The two are not separate issues. It's one phrase. It's not we were shooting at Mujahedin and snipers; we were shooting at Mujahedin snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the text that has been quoted to you that they were shooting at Mujahedin snipers and not just at Mujahedin, that is -- the answer quoted to you is the correct answer and the answer given by you during testimony that they were shooting Mujahedin is an incomplete answer. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying here is that I'm not -- I think -- as I understood the question, that they weren't just shooting at the Mujahedin; they were also shooting at snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question is what the answer is that you heard at that time from the man you put the question to. Did he say, "We're shooting at the Mujahedin," or did he say, "We are shooting at the Mujahedin snipers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, on that occasion he said "Mujahedin snipers." At other moments people simply used the word "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that clarify the issue you're raising, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Or if there's any additional question, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this point, no, but I believe that there is a difference in what the witness stated this morning and what he stated later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, let me return to the question of snipers. And I don't think I heard it from you, but is it true, or do you know if there were sniper units on the side of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were snipers in the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. Just to clarify and specify one point: You were talking about the Mujahedin and you said that you had been to Afghanistan. Is it true to say that when we say "Mujahedin," we are, in principal, talking about the combatants of the holy war? And I'm talking in general.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The word "Mujahedin" means holy warrior. Yes, you're absolutely right. However, it was the Afghan resistance where for the first time in the 1980s the term was widely heard of -- they called themselves the Mujahedin, or in singular, a Mujahed. I have never, throughout my years in Bosnia, heard any member of the Bosnian army refer to himself as a Mujahed or his troops as Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said, sir, also in your written statement that the schools had been closed. Could you confirm this before the Chamber, the schools in Sarajevo, of course.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At the periods that I was in Sarajevo, as far as we were informed, the schools were closed. I went to a number of schools on a number of occasions, and we never found any pupils there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron, you also said this morning, and in your written statement, that you were not satisfied with your first choice of accommodation in Sarajevo and that you changed your accommodation. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When I arrived there in May 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. You also indicated that one of the reasons for which you were dissatisfied was the presence in the vicinity of what, in French, we call the headquarters, HQ.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were in a building, as I described it, which later became the building that Generals Morillon and Roso and others stayed in. It was not "the" headquarters, but it was a building used by what was known at that stage of the conflict as I think the territorial forces of the Bosnians, and it was one of their headquarters. And therefore, we felt that staying in this building, we were close to potential target. Apart from that, there are other reasons, as I have already described. There was a relatively low building. I could not work there at night. If I am in a low building and shells are falling around, like many other people, I became frightened, and that's why we sought a different place to work at at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron, what was the distance between what you have just been describing, that is to say, the QG or [Quatier General], and where you moved to?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You're referring to the military hospital, the former military hospital now known as the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no, that wasn't my question. I do apologise, sir. You were talking about the HQ, and you mentioned a moment ago what was your first place of accommodation, which you refused. Now, between those two points, Point A and Point B, what was the distance between your first initial accommodation and the HQ?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't refuse it. I simply moved. I left my things there throughout the period I was there in May and early June. The distance would have been a few hundred metres. I mean, there's a park around this building, and it's a couple of hundred, maybe two, three hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you be more precise with respect to the distance, to the best of your recollections?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not an area I walked in. We drove in Sarajevo. So it was the next building. It was outside the park. We didn't initially know what this building was. We discovered later that it was a building used by, as I say -- I think called the territorial defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a couple of hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If I understood you correctly, it is that distance of several hundred metres with respect to a potentially military facility that motivated your move, I mean the dangers that this implied of having something close by like that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. The principal reason why we moved is I couldn't work there. There was shelling happening every night in Sarajevo during this period, and I wanted to be able to film it. And I could not do this from this building. That is the principal reason. But there was an added reason because if I had remained in this building, shells could have -- I mean, the -- this base of the territorial defence forces could have become a place of attack, and that was another reason. But the main reason was I couldn't work and do the filming that I wished to do. We wanted to find a high building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron, do you know of other headquarters which might have been situated within the urban limits of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. At different times of the war, there were different buildings that we went to to have contacts with military officers of the Bosnian side. So I'm aware of that there were different offices used within the confines that you mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what areas or what types of areas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the city centre, relatively close to the Bosnian Presidency, and then there were other headquarters further out of -- away from the city centre that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I might ask you to indicate this to us on a map later on, but what types of installations were these? You mentioned several types of locations and military facilities, installations. What types of these were you able to see in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't understand [Quartier General].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That means headquarters, sorry, headquarters, [Quartier General].

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You are only referring to the Bosnian side, not the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The headquarters that we saw were headquarters with offices, possibly operations rooms where operations were planned, but we were obviously not allowed in those. And offices where I could meet either the -- there was a press and information service of the Bosnian -- or officers, including the commanding officer of the Bosnian Army. But this is later on, who I met in -- at the beginning of 1995 at Oslobodenje. I went to his office, and that was in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir. I may have misphrased my question. Let me try to rephrase it. What type of buildings? What type of installations or locations were there, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, these were normal buildings, office buildings. As far as I could judge, these had all previously been office. But also as far as I could judge, they had not previously been military offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Baron, I think I heard you mention that you had been a 2nd Lieutenant in the Dutch army, and I'm now going to ask you a question bearing that fact in mind. Do you know what was the number of personnel in Sarajevo within the so-called Bosnian army? What was the strength of that army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly, I was not there as a Dutch military officer or as a member of any kind of military force or of UNPROFOR, and that has to be made perfectly clear. I left the Dutch military in 1978 before any misunderstanding. Apart from that, I was not in the army; I was in the marine corps. As far as the number of troops, we were never given any figures of that nature by anyone on the Bosnian side or the Bosnian authorities, either civilian or military. I knew the first -- the commander of the 1st Corps, as the unit was called, Mustafa Hajrulahovic. He never gave me figures of that nature. And I couldn't give you a figure of that nature. Certainly within the 1st Corps, I would imagine there were several brigades and several thousand men, but I can't give you a precise figure. You would have to ask somebody from UNPROFOR that kind of question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron, you have already partially responded to my next question, but let me try to be more specific. You told us that there was the 1st Corps of the army in Sarajevo and that there were several brigades within that corps. Could you tell us what would have been the strength of such a brigade? Or rather, generally speaking, what is the strength of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When the war began, there was no Bosnian army. And you should realise that in asking these questions. Therefore, while, during the war, the Bosnian army tried to organise itself along the classical lines of the army, along -- in fact, along the ways that most of its officers who had been formerly in the JNA had been taught to do. Unit strength was often quite different than I would expect. I would expect a brigade to include four, maybe five battalions; maybe less, it depends. Different armies do it in a different way. Each battalion would be made up of three or four companies. These companies would usually have a strength of anywhere between 150 and 180 men. This was not always the case either on the Bosnian side or on the Bosnian Serb side. So, I mean, it's an impossible question that you're asking. I can't give those precise figures, because you're also dealing, specifically on the Bosnian side, with an army which developed as the war went along. So at different times, the figures would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I fully understand that, Baron, but perhaps when you don't know something, you can simply respond by saying "I don't know." I'm saying this only for practical purposes so that we can move on. I'm now going to refer myself to something that you testified about this morning, in particular, what you said at 9.26.12. I believe we were on page 11 of the Livenote. You stated that "Serbs had scattered their artillery pieces because they were afraid that they had spread them" -- "actually because they were afraid that their opponents could return fire." That is, that they were fearful of being hit. My question in relation to that is as follows: Can I, therefore, conclude, that the Bosnian army also had artillery pieces at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: First things first: The position was a normal military position. If the Bosnian Serbs had stuck all their artillery together, it would have been outrageous. And I wouldn't expect an army led by professional soldiers to have done that. Secondly, did they have artillery? Hardly. They did. I am aware that they did have heavy mortars. I am referring to 120 millimetre mortars. I never personally saw any artillery of the Bosnian army inside Sarajevo. But I did see 120 millimetre mortars because at a certain moment in February 1994, there were also weapon collection points set up in Sarajevo. And I visited one of those once I reached the city. But I never saw any artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron Van Lynden, haven't you ever seen, yes or no, a tank at the Bosnian army side?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, but a tank couldn't have fired at this artillery position. Only artillery could have fired back. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I agree. But I think I can conclude from your answer, and I should like to ask you to confirm that, that the Bosnian army troops had at least a tank.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you know, what type of tank that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it was a T65. No M84s. The Yugoslav version of the T72.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Baron. Let me now move to an incident that you have spoken about, the buildings, the apartment blocks situated along Marsal Tito Bulevar. When you gave your written statement which you subsequently signed, you indicated to the interviewer that the building that you had seen had already been on fire. Is it correct? Baron, am I right in saying that, therefore, consequently, you were not able to see the beginning of the attack?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I mean, there was fire -- I mean smoke was already rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand what you mean. Thank you. Since you didn't see the beginning of the attack, am I correct in saying that you were not able to see what could have happened before the incident, just before the incident?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I said, I was in a car driving -- yes. But as I've also explained, we asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm also trying to be as brief as possible, Baron. I hope you understand me. In your statement, you also said - and I should like to have your confirmation - of that, that as far as this particular incident is concerned, one could not completely exclude the possibility that the building was being used for sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence would like the witness to comment, make a comment on what he said in the witness statement, that he either be shown the witness statement so he can see it or that he just read out the one sentence in full of which you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's preferable. I do agree with you, Mr. Waespi. On the other hand, if you could check and if there's no dispute as to the correctness of the summary which is contained in the question, I'd rather not to come back to it later. But in general, I do agree with you that we prefer literal quoting. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin does know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's an important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's an important issue, so I would rather have him quote the one or two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, maybe we could be allowed to show the document to the witness. He can perhaps identify his signature on the document and read aloud the portion in question. It is a matter of several lines. By proceeding that way, we will authenticate the document and the witness will be able to read directly from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we had some discussions about context of statements. Statements will have to be either marked for identification or to be tendered into evidence. So if it would be possible just to read the lines relevant to your question, that would be highly preferable, in my view. But if you insist, of course, I can't keep you off from tendering the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer, Mr. President, for the witness to read the relevant passage. We will thereby be able to confirm what he had declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber cannot check whether this is a correct reading or not, since we have not the document. So if the Prosecution and the Defence -- I mean, you have to go there, you have to indicate, you have to give it to the usher, which is highly impractical. If you state just the lines you're referring to and if the Prosecution checks whether this is a literal quoting, then we can continue. That's what I really prefer. And I think the Prosecution has at its desk the statement, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So please quote, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Do you want me to give the document to the Prosecution or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Page 10, you stated, sir, and I quote: [In English] "... the use of this building by ABiH snipers. There is no way, in my opinion, that the attack could have been justifiable military action." [Interpretation] I've just quoted from your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is not complete in this respect. Could you please read the line again, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "One cannot exclude the use ..." So I check with the transcript. "... the use of this building by ABiH snipers. There is no way, in my opinion, that the attack could have been a justifiable military action."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I stand by what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Therefore, there must have been a theoretical possibility for such a battalion [as interpreted] in Sarajevo to have been used as a sniper position by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The translation here is all over the place, because you mean batiment, not battalion, I take it. It's written --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] I mean batiment.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You mean building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I mean buildings, of course.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the translation is incorrect. Yes, there is absolutely a theoretical possibility that such buildings could have been used by snipers of the Bosnian army. I can't exclude that, no. That's what I wrote in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's okay. That's okay. I didn't -- [Interpretation] Baron van Lynden, you have spoken about an attack on the UNIS company buildings in Sarajevo in your statement; is that correct? Sir, could you please tell us whether this UNIS towers were indeed high-rise buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us how many floors there were, approximately? Approximately, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Approximately 35, 40. I don't -- I mean, I didn't count the floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Baron. Were they positioned in such a way that one could have a very good view of the city from there? I'm still talking about the UNIS towers.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could one imagine the possibility that these buildings could have been used as firing positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You could imagine it, but I actually went into one of them two days before the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated and, as I recall now, four or five days before one of the UNIS towers was almost completely destroyed by fire. There was a problem if you used it as a shoot-out. As far as I could see, all the windows were fixed. It was one of these modern blocks relying on air-conditioning. And apart from that, I never, at any time when we were staying in the military hospital, or what later became known as the State Hospital, which is very close by the two UNIS towers, I never saw any outgoing fire from either of them. They could also have been used, just to make the point more clearly, while the Marsal Tito barracks were still inhabited by forces of the Bosnian Serbs. They could have been used to shoot into the military barracks, because they had a direct view inside those barracks. And when we went into the UNIS towers, it was for the reason to be able to film inside the Marsal Tito barracks, which we did. But as I mentioned, we couldn't open the windows. We had to film through the glass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are at a point where we should have a break. Would you please find a suitable moment somewhere in the next one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be a convenient moment, and we will be able to discuss this problem concerning exhibits with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we have a break, I noticed that sometimes there emerges some kind of a debate between the witness and the Defence, and I would ask the witness to give answers to what the Defence has asked, and if there's anything additional which is of such an importance that it should be said, that you address the Chamber and ask whether, apart from having given the answer to the Defence, you could make any additional remarks. But I'd like to prevent debate between counsel and witnesses. So we'll then adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I hope that the copying problem has been solved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, I would like to return to some technical questions. Did you notice what type of uniforms were worn by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At different moments, different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did this Bosnian army also have, among its staff, among its troops, professional officers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago, Baron van Lynden, a name in relation to the 1st Corps of the army stationed in Sarajevo, and these professional officers, did they -- they normally came from the former JNA, from the former Yugoslav People's Army. I am referring in particular to what you declared regarding the 1st Corps of the army.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. As I am aware. Mustafa Hajrulahovic had served as a professional officer in the Yugoslav People's Army, and other officers had also served in that army. I'm not aware of them having served in any other army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a moment ago several questions regarding some facilities or buildings of HQs in the city of Sarajevo. Do you remember? For the transcript, could you please say your answer.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember you asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be in a position to indicate for us on a map these locations regarding the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm certainly willing to try. As I said before, there are several buildings. They weren't always headquarters. They could be local headquarters, let's say. And I could certainly try, but I'm not sure that -- you know, how accurate I would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would it be possible to have a map available to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps the witness could use a different colour, perhaps black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing against the colour black.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- just make the point that this is a very rough map. I mean, that is not a map that any motorist entering Sarajevo would use to find their way, and therefore my locations are very general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think you couldn't properly identify the locations on this map, I would suggest that we use another one. I cannot blame the Defence for not having prepared it. But if you would have another one --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not have here before us a map, but unfortunately it's already been -- markings have already been made on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may suggest, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's just try to see how far we come and how precise we can be, and if it turns out to be insufficiently precise, then we still can change to another map. So if you please -- you have got a black marker? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, could you please indicate on this map the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. locations, as far as you know, the headquarters of the 1st Corps of the army.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot state that this was the headquarters of the 1st Corps of the army. I know of a building where I met Mustafa Hajrulahovic. I don't know if that was the headquarters or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you cannot indicate it. Could you indicate on this map different locations that you were aware of and that would correspond to the HQ or military facilities?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Do your best.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first place I would like to mention is this territorial army headquarters or base close to my first port of call or first port of stay in Sarajevo that was mentioned, in May. And as I'm aware, it would be -- how would you like me to mark it, with a T or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you can guide the witness in the marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I think that we will use numbers. If you can just mark number 1 in Arabic numbers on this location.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Arabic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Arabic numerals, not Roman numerals. Figures, just normal numbers.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The second is the place where I -- it's there roughly. I mean this is the rough area I'm doing. This is not precise. The second area I would like to mark with number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please, sir -- sir, could you please make a circle around the location. We cannot see it very well.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Using a chronological listing of numbers, we continue.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The second would be where I met Mustafa Hajrulahovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, if that's how you want it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is very general. It is a small street. And the third that I can mark is the rough location of the building where I met Rasim Delic in early 1995. I have to reiterate that this is very rough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have repeatedly said so, and it's quite well understood. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, could you please -- about the headquarters that were near your first accommodation, could you indicate it? Your first accommodation, so the facility that you moved from. So we're talking about Number 1.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if -- could you indicate or would you be able to indicate on this map where the Holiday Inn hotel is on this map?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Do you want to mark that with a 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, what is the approximate distance as far as you know between the Holiday Inn hotel, number 4 on this map, and the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They are almost adjacent to each other. They are very close. It depends which part of Marsal Tito barracks, because it's a large establishment. But they are very close to each other. The "T" on the map that I put earlier is my recollection of the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, do you know if at any time following the month of September 1992 the Holiday Inn hotel could have been used also for purposes of having that as military offices?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You do not know. You never heard it said that there were offices, military offices, there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I recall. I didn't stay at the Holiday Inn. Most journalists did, but I never stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I would like to return to the period of time when you told us that you arrived, in May 1992, in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I arrived in Sarajevo in May 1992. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You told me, Baron van Lynden, that at first, the Bosnian army was not perfectly well organised. Did I understand you correctly, or it was not perfectly structured?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When the war began, there was no Bosnian army. And therefore, it only slowly started to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, am I right to say that at the start of the hostilities, the Bosnian forces did not have at their disposal many military structures?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I said, I only got there in May. I was not there in April. As far as I'm aware, their initial structure was based on the police and on the territorial defence forces, my --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is also regarding May. My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your question was whether at the start of the hostilities, so I think the witness is perfectly right in -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, at the time when you arrived, which is very shortly after the beginning of the hostilities, in May 1992 -- and I can rephrase the question, but it's the same question, so the time after you arrived.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Their structures were weak. In as far as they existed, they were weak structures; although I did, in my first visit to Sarajevo, encounter a semblance of organisation. But absolutely not to the same effect that one did even in the autumn of 1992. Things had clearly already changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Sir, you stated in your statement that I'm referring to - and this is still the same statement - that there were many men who were held in Sarajevo, a large number of men in the Bosnian army, that were held in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, please indicate at least on which page of the statement and then perhaps quote the one or two sentences you are referring to. Even I can't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, literal quoting is to be preferred. Please quote literally, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. This is page 5. And I have here the translation, and this is a Serbian translation of the statement, and this is exactly what I am referring to. So I will now try and find the English text which should be found approximately on the same page. And I'm going to quote in English. You said the following: [In English] "It was easy to keep under siege, as the topography allowed relatively few infantry forces, backed up by artillery, to keep large numbers of Bosnian troops committed to the defence of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the use of -- the term that you used yourself, so the term "large numbers." We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you are talking about large numbers of soldiers - and we do know that you are not able to give us a precise figure, and that is normal - do you know where, in general, these soldiers were, where their positions were in the city itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: On the front lines, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there locations in the city where the soldiers were able to withdraw to? Because obviously they were not able to stay on the front line the entire time.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, when Bosnian soldiers were in their positions, they were in their positions. It's not a question of a 9 to 5 job that you go home in the evening. If they were allowed to go home, those who had homes in Sarajevo -- because, of course, there were also refugees who had come to Sarajevo who also formed part of their army. Then they - this was if they'd be given two or three days or longer - then they went home. I'm not aware of major barracks, if that's what you're referring to, inside the city. I'm not aware of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you do not know about any particular quarters where they were staying?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any major Bosnian army barracks during the war within the city. I'm aware that most soldiers were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. Baron van Lynden, we are still talking about the city of Sarajevo. Could you tell us about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the transcript, page 83, number 14, I think that the witness said: "I am aware that most soldiers were --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. I think this has been corrected properly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am sorry. I apologise. I am not following the transcript. Perhaps I should. But I'm going to ask my question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, the question was the following: You just told us about the front lines in the city of Sarajevo. What was the length, as far as you know, approximately, the length of the front lines in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a figure of how many kilometres the front lines were. War correspondents don't go around the front lines counting how long the front line is. It was all around the city. The city was besieged. And it's not straight lines either. So I cannot give you a figure. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Baron van Lynden, I'm going to return to the question of equipment. Did you know -- do you know whether, when you arrived, so almost the beginning of the war in 1992, whether the Bosnian troops were issued uniforms on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, at that time some of the troops did have uniform. I saw others who had no uniform, who were simply in civilian clothes. As I have already said, there was no Bosnian army, and therefore it was only much later that you saw whole units all wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said - but I'm just going to check on the transcript - you said a moment ago that the others were not wearing uniform. You were talking about soldiers, talking about troops?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There were armed people. Whether they knew precisely whether they were in a -- they were not in a brigade, a company, that we would normally associate with an army maybe at that stage, but they were certainly armed and they were wearing either a bit of a uniform or civilian clothes. Some were fully uniformed. It was a mishmash.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Baron van Lynden. Perhaps you could reply directly to the Chamber rather than to me, so that perhaps we can avoid having dialogues. Baron van Lynden -- I'm sorry. I'm rephrasing that. Did you hear, sir, that on the Serbian side, civilian victims were caused -- or were victims of Bosnian snipers, that is, that they were victims caused by the other side?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Hear, yes; see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you never report in your reports that there was also sniping -- that there was Bosnian sniping - and I'm talking about, obviously, other incidents in the war - that there was a Serbian civilian population that were victims?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We reported that there were civilian casualties. But as I said, I never saw them. We heard from the civilian population when I was in Grbavica, that they were sniped at, and we did report that, but I was never taken to a hospital and shown civilian casualties. So I personally didn't see it, but we did hear it, we were told it, and yes, we reported what we had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I understand well that you said that you never saw with your own eyes civilians who were victims from snipers.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, could you tell us, please, and indicate on the map that you have to your right, the Dobrinja area. Could you mark that in, even if it is only roughly.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Shall I mark it number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you first show us the general area.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
